newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians say Israel killing peace process.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians say Israel killing peace process.

text.p: Officials of Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority said on Friday that Israel was killing the peace process and demanded that the Palestinian president suspend negotiations with the Jewish state.
Palestinians have been enraged over Israel's decision last month to build a Jewish settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim, known in Israel as Har Homa, in Arab East Jerusalem.

They were further disappointed when Netanyahu's government decided to hand over only two percent of the 70 percent of the West Bank still under exclusive Israeli control to the PLO under a peace deal.
Another seven percent of the West bank would be transferred from joint Israel-PLO rule to Palestinian control, under the proposal narrowly approved overnight by Israel's cabinet.

"What the Israeli government has done with its decision is kill this (peace) process," said Palestinian Legislative Council speaker Ahmed Korei, who negotiated the broad 1993 self-rule peace deal with Israel.

"Personally, I think it is shameful to continue to say that there is a peace process. It is shameful to continue to sit at the negotiations table under these conditions and with this kind of mentality," he told Israel Radio.
Asked if he was proposing to stop the negotiations, he said: "Without any doubt."
Arafat, who returned to Gaza from Washington on Friday, was due to convene his cabinet and the PLO executive committee to discuss the Israeli decision.
But Palestinians said Arafat was unlikely to heed calls to suspend the negotiations at this stage.
Israel and the PLO are due to resume talks later this month on a permanent peace deal covering the future of Jerusalem, the fate of Jewish settlements and the boundaries of a Palestinian entity.

Palestinians, who have set up limited self rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip under the 1993 accord, hope that the talks, scheduled to last until 1999, would culminate in the establishment of an independent state.
Salah al-Taamari, a lawmaker said: "The Palestinian side may not be able to deploy tanks, jets and rockets. But I think that the Palestinian leadership can stop the negotiations."

"President Arafat can stand and tell his people and the world that we have given peace every possible chance and that these negotiations have become an umbrella used by the Israelis to dictate to the Palestinian people," he said.
Arafat, who has insisted during his visit to Washington on the need to safeguard the peace process, voiced disappointment with the Israeli decision.
"This is a big deceit operation. It came from one party, without consultation with us," Arafat told reporters in Gaza upon his return home from a visit to the United States.

Arafat aide Tayeb Abdel-Rahim said under the peace deals, Israel was obliged to give the Palestinians 30 percent of the land still under its control during each of the three stages of further redeployment agreed upon under the 1995 self-rule deal.
"The latest decision is a violation of the agreement and we do not accept it," Abdel-Rahim told the radio.

"I am a centrist, but it seems that we must reevaluate the negotiations to correct its path. The negotiations are deviating from its true path and therefore one has to be with those who say that we should re-evaluate the situation anew."

Earlier, Saeb Erekat, minister of local government in the Palestinian Authority and a peace negotiator, told Israel Radio: "I think we are facing a real crisis in the peace process now and when I say a real crisis I mean it."
